title: Tessellation
sub: How finely to slice exact geometry
cards/0/title: To show CAD, you cut it into triangles
cards/0/body:
A GPU cannot draw “cylinder R50”. So before display, exact geometry is tessellated: turned into triangles.

The main question is how finely.
cards/1/task: Get the deviation from the true cylinder down to 0.1 mm or less, using no more than 260 triangles. Spin the cylinder with your finger.
cards/2/body:
A straight segment in place of an arc is a chord. The largest distance between the arc and the chord is the sagitta (chord height): r · (1 − cos(π / n)).

Double the segments and the error drops about fourfold, while the triangle count doubles.
cards/3/q: There were 32 segments, now there are 64. How did the error change?
cards/3/explain: For large n the sagitta ≈ r·π²/(2n²): the error falls with the square of the segment count.
cards/4/q: How does the size of a STEP file with this cylinder change between coarse and fine tessellation?
cards/4/options/0: Not at all: STEP holds the formula, and tessellation happens later, at display or export
cards/4/options/1: It grows with the triangle count
cards/4/explain: A STEP file’s size depends on the part’s complexity, not on display quality.
cards/5/body:
When CAD exports to STL or glTF, you set tolerances. Chordal deviation is how far triangles may stray from the surface, in millimeters. Angular deviation is how much neighboring triangles may differ in slope.

Tight tolerances give smooth and heavy; loose ones give light and angular.
cards/5/deep: The angular tolerance saves small features: for a Ø2 mm hole, a 0.1 mm chordal deviation gives only 7 segments, and the angle forces more. For the web, 0.1–0.5 mm is often enough. Huge assemblies get LODs (several levels of detail) or streaming formats like 3D Tiles.
cards/6/q: What grows when you tighten the tessellation tolerance? Select all.
cards/6/options/3: Accuracy of the source CAD model
cards/6/explain: The source CAD model is exact already. Only its approximation changes.
cards/7/q: A CAD part’s path to a website
cards/8/q: A Ø2 mm hole looks like a heptagon at a 0.1 mm chordal tolerance. What helps?
cards/8/options/0: Add an angular tolerance: it forces small circles to be split finer
cards/8/options/2: Save as OBJ instead of STL
cards/8/explain: The chordal tolerance suits large arcs; the angular one suits small ones.
